Sixteen comments

The Cameronian

Another widely played session tune, and rightfully so.

Watch for those back to back Bs when going from measure 2 to 3 and again from 6 to 7. On fiddle, I do these with on one bow stroke with a cut note (flick of the ring finger) to separate them into the two eighth notes. This helps keep the flow going.

↳ Posted by Will Harmon on September 17th, 2001.

Odd b

Sorry, Jeremy. That b in the opening two notes is supposed to be “B,” the next octave down. I fixed the abc…hope it isn’t too big a job to repair the sheet music and midi….
Thanks,
Will

↳ Posted by Will Harmon on September 17th, 2001.

Rant

I think this tune has is origins (don’t they all) in an old Scottish tune, the Cameronian Rant, found in the Atholl Collection. It was obviously adapted to the Irish reel structure, and transposed to D from its original key of F.

↳ Posted by CreadurMawnOrganig on September 20th, 2001.

The Cameronian, X:6

This version appears in P.W. Joyce’s Old Irish Music and Songs (1909), vol. 1, p. 114-115, No. 236, as Carey’s Dream.
Joyce wrote that he copied it from two very old well-written manuscripts lent to him in 1873 by Mr J. O’Sullivan, of Bruff, Co. Limerick.

↳ Posted by Moxhe on November 2nd, 2015.

The Cameronian, X:8

A slightly different setting with some dotted notes, giving it that Scottish feel. This version was - I’m fairly sure - collected in the north of Ireland in the 1980’s, so maybe the dotted notes reflect the regional style. Taken from ‘A Fine Selection of Over 200 Irish Traditional Tunes for Sessions’, compiled by David Speers with a Forward by Matt Cranitch.

↳ Posted by Eubonian on January 24th, 2019.

Fermanagh Version from Pat McManus

Pat McManus played the following version on a private tape. I like the C natural section in the B-part. He said his sources for the tune were Tim Healy and Johnny McQuaid whom I presume are older generation Fermanagh musicians long since gone. Though I never heard of them personally.

EDIT: I’ve just added it via the “Add setting” section.
